summary: MoFlow (IBM and Notre Dame) searches for agentic workflow graphs that trade off five objectives (accuracy, token cost, latency in sequential calls, robustness to paraphrase, run-to-run consistency). Workflow construction is cast as a multi-objective MDP and solved with Convex-Hull Monte Carlo Tree Search whose nodes store sets of reachable trade-offs, so one search covers the convex Pareto front and any preference is served by lookup. An online variant executes every candidate; an offline variant uses a GNN value model pretrained on the online runs' execution data. Against six AFlow-family generators (AFlow, MaAS, FlowSteer, SkillFlow, ADAS, EvoMAS), each rerun per preference, on six benchmarks (AIME 2026, MATH-Hard, MBPP, SWE-Bench Lite, GPQA-Diamond, HotpotQA-Hard; 20-50 held-out problems each), MoFlow has the best mean hypervolume (24.02 online, 24.43 offline vs 21.66 for ADAS) and wins on 4 of 6 benchmarks, often by small margins, with one seed. Per-query search yields workflows costing 1.1-11.6x the tokens of a per-task workflow with no gain. The study cost about 12B tokens (~$14,700). Code is public.

claims.claim: Under a setup that favors the baselines (rerun for each test preference), MoFlow achieves the highest average hypervolume
claims.evidence: Table 2 mean HV 24.02 (online) and 24.43 (offline) vs ADAS 21.66 and EvoMAS 21.63; best on 4 of 6 benchmarks, with small margins on some (SWE-Bench Lite 7.54 vs 7.30, GPQA 20.39 vs 20.17). The +/- values are SD across benchmarks, not across runs, and there is one seed. 'Favors the baselines' is arguable: baselines get 5.6-28.7M tokens per preference (62-316M per benchmark over eleven preferences), while one online MoFlow search spends 116-597M.
claims.location: Abstract, §5 (Main results), Table 2, App. D (Total cost)

claims.claim: Offline MoFlow matches online quality at about 2% of the search cost, a significant saving vs the baselines
claims.evidence: Offline search uses 2.9-3.6M proposer/realizer tokens, but its GNN is pretrained on execution data the online searches collected on the same six tasks; that cost is excluded from the comparison.
AIME 2026 only (Table 3): first on GPT-5 Mini, second on Claude Haiku 4.5, Gemini 3 Flash Preview and DeepSeek-V4-Flash; best mean and best worst-case (16.09). One benchmark, one seed.

claims.claim: Query-level (per-query) search does not produce better workflows than task-level search
claims.evidence: Same method and settings on all six benchmarks: per-query trees cost 0.6-0.9x a task-level tree to build, but their workflows use 1.1-11.6x the tokens and 1.1-6.6x the sequential calls per problem with no gain on other objectives; held-out/in-sample HV ratio as low as 0.28 vs >=0.66 for task-level trees.

claims.claim: Contextual-zooming action selection gives the best hypervolume at lowest cost
claims.evidence: Ablation vs three other selection rules on AIME 2026 with Claude Haiku 4.5 only (Table 4).

patterns.note: Searched workflow generation with Pareto-set backups. It is compared only with other workflow-search methods (best mean HV, one seed); no hand-written workflow, single-call or plain agent-loop baseline tests whether searching for a workflow beats not searching.

The output is a static workflow graph fixed per task and preference, chosen by lookup at inference. It is not compared with a plain agent loop or with a hand-designed fixed graph, so whether a static graph helps is not tested.

Closest evidence: per-query graph generation (an LLM-proposed workflow built for each query via a small search tree) vs one fixed per-task graph, same method and benchmarks. Per-query workflows cost 1.1-11.6x the tokens and 1.1-6.6x the calls with no gain and overfit more (App. A.2). This leans against generating a graph per task instance, but it is offline search with executions, not a planner emitting a DAG at run time, and it uses one seed.
Token cost and sequential-call latency are first-class objectives, and total study cost is disclosed (~12B tokens, ~$14,700); no comparison with a budget-capped agent.
Hypervolume over five objectives with paraphrase robustness and repeat consistency is a richer evaluation than accuracy alone, but it is aggregated over 20-50 held-out problems per benchmark.

methodology.sample: Six benchmarks, 10-20 build and 20-50 held-out problems each; each workflow run six times per problem (3 repeats + 3 paraphrases)
methodology.baselines: AFlow, MaAS, FlowSteer, SkillFlow, ADAS, EvoMAS, each rerun per preference (eleven preferences) at default budgets
methodology.models: GPT-5 Mini (main), plus Claude Haiku 4.5, Gemini 3 Flash Preview and DeepSeek-V4-Flash on AIME 2026
methodology.variance: Single seed; repeat and paraphrase variance is folded into objectives, not reported as uncertainty on HV; table +/- is SD across benchmarks
methodology.ablations: Action-selection rule (AIME, one model); preference-conditioned selection; query- vs task-level search; online vs offline
methodology.contamination_controls: Build/held-out split; AIME 2026 is recent; MATH, MBPP, HotpotQA, SWE-Bench Lite are public and likely seen
methodology.languages: Python (MBPP, SWE-Bench Lite); math and QA

standards.artifacts: Code at github.com/yining610/MoFlow; hyperparameters and seed in App. D

biases.detail: One seed; no CIs on hypervolume despite small per-benchmark margins.
20-50 held-out problems per benchmark; cross-model claim rests on AIME alone.
Code benchmarks are MBPP and SWE-Bench Lite, both Python.
Workflows are searched on 10-20 build problems from the same benchmark and operator pools are hand-designed per task (App. B).
Table +/- is SD across benchmarks, which can be misread as run variance.
The offline variant's low search cost excludes the online execution data, from the same tasks, used to pretrain its value model.

coi.affiliations: IBM (four authors); University of Notre Dame
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and DeepSeek models as backbones; no IBM product
coi.detail: Vendor affiliation only; no IBM product is graded.

verdict_reason: A well-specified method with open code, disjoint held-out sets, multi-objective evaluation and an honest cost disclosure. The caveats: one seed with small margins, comparisons only within the workflow-search family, and two pieces of framing that overstate the case (baselines 'favored' despite similar total compute, offline 'cheap' excluding its training data).
applicability: Weak relevance to the Java team. The useful finding for the DAG question is the query-level vs task-level result: a single workflow fixed per task type was as good as generating a workflow per instance and used up to ~12x fewer tokens per problem. That favours a small library of fixed per-task-type workflows (for example ingest-new-content-source or regenerate-client-DTOs) over having an LLM build a fresh graph for every request. The search machinery itself (thousands of executions, ~12B tokens in the study) is research infrastructure, not something a product team should run, and nothing here is Java or multi-repo.

conflicts_with.detail: Same batch, apparent tension: MoFlow finds per-query graph generation adds cost without gain, whereas DAGent's per-query DAG, grown from intermediate evidence, beats linear loops and an upfront plan in deep research. A likely reconciliation is that DAGent conditions on evidence during execution while MoFlow's per-query search chooses a graph before execution.

Same batch: ROGUE's permutation study suggests its searched workflow mostly recovers a fixed coarse-to-fine cascade, a reminder that searched workflows should be compared with simple fixed ones, which MoFlow does not do.
